expectedText:
SPECIAL ADMINISTRATOR OF A DECEDENT'S ESTATE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan Rivera · August 12, 2026

PURPOSE OF THIS SPECIAL ADMINISTRATOR INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the special administrator of a decedent's estate under California law — a person a probate court may appoint on a temporary, emergency basis to protect and manage a decedent's estate before a general personal representative (executor or administrator) is appointed and issued Letters. It is prepared in connection with Pat Morgan Rivera's estate, who died on August 12, 2026, based on the following circumstances said to require immediate protection of the estate before a general personal representative can be appointed: Perishable inventory in a decedent-owned business requires immediate management. Jordan Lee is the person proposed for appointment as special administrator, and this information sheet is intended for use with a petition to be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of Alameda County. This information sheet is not itself a petition, and preparing or signing it does not appoint Jordan Lee — or anyone else — special administrator of Pat Morgan Rivera's estate, does not itself preserve or protect any estate property, and does not itself give Jordan Lee any authority to act for the estate. Only a court order, followed by issuance of letters, does that. This document addresses only the special administrator's temporary, emergency role under Probate Code Division 7, Part 2, Chapter 4, Article 8 (§§ 8540-8547); it does not address the separate process for appointing a general personal representative described in this project's Petition for Probate — Information Sheet.

WHEN A COURT MAY APPOINT A SPECIAL ADMINISTRATOR, AND HOW THE APPOINTMENT ORDER IS STRUCTURED
Probate Code § 8540(a) provides that if the circumstances of Pat Morgan Rivera's estate require the immediate appointment of a personal representative, the court may appoint a special administrator to exercise any powers that may be appropriate under the circumstances for the preservation of the estate. § 8540(b) separately provides that the appointment may be for a specified term, to perform particular acts, or on any other terms specified in the court order — meaning the scope and duration of a special administrator's role is set by the individual court order appointing that person, not by a single fixed statutory role that looks the same in every case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) If the circumstances of the estate require the immediate appointment of a personal representative, the court may appoint a special administrator to exercise any powers that may be appropriate under the circumstances for the preservation of the estate. (b) The appointment may be for a specified term, to perform particular acts, or on any other terms specified in the court order."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8540 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8540 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8540.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes both subsections of a single statutory section (§ 8540(a) and § 8540(b)) as one citation; they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, and not a claim that any particular estate's circumstances meet this statute's 'immediate appointment' trigger. Special Administrators appear in Probate Code Division 7, Part 2, Chapter 4, Article 8 (§§ 8540-8547) — confirmed directly from the Probate Code's own table of contents at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which places this article after Article 7 (Changes in Administration, §§ 8520-8525) and before Article 9 (Nonresident Personal Representative, §§ 8570-8577), within the same Part 2 chapter that governs appointment of the general personal representative. This document does not separately address the bond a court may require of a special administrator (§§ 8480-8488, 8543) or the letters-and-oath issuance mechanics for a special administrator (§ 8542). This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any special administrator or determine that immediate appointment is warranted for any specific estate — only a court order does that.

NOTICE IS NOT REQUIRED FOR APPOINTMENT, AND THE COURT'S PREFERENCE AMONG CANDIDATES
Probate Code § 8541(a) provides that appointment of a special administrator may be made at any time without notice, or on such notice to interested persons as the court deems reasonable — unlike the notice-and-hearing process this project's companion Petition for Probate — Information Sheet describes for appointment of a general personal representative, the statute leaves whether to require notice, and how much, to the court's own discretion rather than mandating notice in every case. § 8541(b) directs that in making the appointment, the court shall ordinarily give preference to the person entitled to appointment as personal representative, and that the court may instead appoint the public administrator. § 8541(c) allows a request for approval of a particular act to be included in the petition for appointment when the appointment is for a particular act, decided on the same notice and at the same time as the appointment itself. § 8541(d) allows the court to act, if necessary, to remedy errors made in the appointment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) Appointment of a special administrator may be made at any time without notice or on such notice to interested persons as the court deems reasonable. (b) In making the appointment, the court shall ordinarily give preference to the person entitled to appointment as personal representative. The court may appoint the public administrator. (c) In the case of an appointment to perform a particular act, request for approval of the act may be included in the petition for appointment, and approval may be made on the same notice and at the same time as the appointment. (d) The court may act, if necessary, to remedy any errors made in the appointment."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8541 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8541 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8541.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes all four subsections of a single statutory section (§ 8541(a)-(d)) as one citation; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text uses the phrase 'without notice,' not 'ex parte'; this clause uses the statute's own language. This clause describes the court's statutory authority to dispense with or limit notice — it is not a claim that any particular petition for appointment of a special administrator will, or should, be granted without notice; that remains within the court's discretion on the facts before it. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any special administrator — only a court order does that.

A SPECIAL ADMINISTRATOR'S POWERS ARE LIMITED BY DEFAULT — NOT THE SAME AS A GENERAL PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE'S UNLESS THE COURT GRANTS MORE
A special administrator's powers over Pat Morgan Rivera's estate are narrower than a general personal representative's by default, and are defined largely by the court's own order rather than by statute alone. Probate Code § 8544(a) provides that except to the extent the order appointing a special administrator prescribes terms, the special administrator has the power to do the following without further order of the court: take possession of the estate's real and personal property and preserve it from damage, waste, and injury; collect claims, rents, and other income belonging to the estate; commence and maintain or defend suits and other legal proceedings; and sell perishable property. § 8544(b) separately lists further powers — including borrowing money or leasing, mortgaging, or executing a deed of trust on real property, and paying interest or other amounts on an obligation secured by a mortgage, lien, or deed of trust on estate property under specified circumstances — that a special administrator has only on order of the court, not automatically. § 8544(c) provides that except where the powers, duties, and obligations of a general personal representative are granted under § 8545, the special administrator is not a proper party to an action on a claim against Pat Morgan Rivera. Probate Code § 8545(a) allows the court to grant a special administrator the same powers, duties, and obligations as a general personal representative where to do so appears proper, but requires that grant — where letters have not previously been issued to a general personal representative — to be made on the same notice required under § 8003 for appointment of a personal representative, unless made at a hearing on a petition for appointment of a general personal representative for which that § 8003 notice has already been given.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) Except to the extent the order appointing a special administrator prescribes terms, the special administrator has the power to do all of the following without further order of the court: (1) Take possession of all of the real and personal property of the estate of the decedent and preserve it from damage, waste, and injury. (2) Collect all claims, rents, and other income belonging to the estate. (3) Commence and maintain or defend suits and other legal proceedings. (4) Sell perishable property. (b) Except to the extent the order prescribes terms, the special administrator has the power to do all of the following on order of the court: (1) Borrow money, or lease, mortgage, or execute a deed of trust on real property, in the same manner as an administrator. (2) Pay the interest due or all or any part of an obligation secured by a mortgage, lien, or deed of trust on property in the estate, where there is danger that the holder of the security may enforce or foreclose on the obligation and the property exceeds in value the amount of the obligation. This power may be ordered only on petition of the special administrator or any interested person, with any notice that the court deems proper, and shall remain in effect until appointment of a successor personal representative. The order may also direct that interest not yet accrued be paid as it becomes due, and the order shall remain in effect and cover the future interest unless and until for good cause set aside or modified by the court in the same manner as for the original order. (3) Exercise other powers that are conferred by order of the court. (c) Except where the powers, duties, and obligations of a general personal representative are granted under Section 8545, the special administrator is not a proper party to an action on a claim against the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8544 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8544 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8544.)
  "(a) Notwithstanding Section 8544, the court may grant a special administrator the same powers, duties, and obligations as a general personal representative where to do so appears proper. Notwithstanding Section 8541, if letters have not previously been issued to a general personal representative, the grant shall be on the same notice required under Section 8003 for appointment of a personal representative, unless the appointment is made at a hearing on a petition for appointment of a general personal representative and the notice of that petition required under Section 8003 has been given."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8545(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8545(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8545.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two different, independently-numbered statutory sections (§ 8544 and § 8545). The central, easily overclaimed point this clause is written to avoid: a special administrator does not automatically have all the powers of a general personal representative; by default under § 8544(a)-(c), those powers are limited to the specific enumerated actions listed above (plus whatever the court's own appointment order additionally prescribes), and the broader powers, duties, and obligations of a general personal representative are available only if the court affirmatively grants them under § 8545, on the notice that section requires. This clause does not quote § 8544(d) (which provides that a special administrator appointed to perform a particular act has no duty to take any other action to protect the estate) or § 8545(b)-(c) (governing an additional bond the court may require as a condition of an § 8545 grant, and the requirement that letters recite the grant); both are honestly disclosed here rather than described. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself grant any powers to any special administrator — only a court order does that.

WHEN A SPECIAL ADMINISTRATOR'S AUTHORITY ENDS, AND THE DUTY TO DELIVER PROPERTY AND ACCOUNT
Probate Code § 8546(a) provides that the powers of a special administrator cease on issuance of letters to a general personal representative, or as otherwise directed by the court. § 8546(b) then requires the special administrator to promptly deliver to the general personal representative all estate property in the special administrator's possession (subject to the court's authority to let the special administrator complete a pending sale or other transaction), and a list of all creditor claims known to the special administrator — showing each creditor's name and address, the claim amount, and what action has been taken on the claim — with a copy of that list filed with the court. § 8546(c) requires the special administrator to account in the same manner as a general personal representative is required to account, and allows that account to be combined with the general personal representative's first account when the same person has held both roles.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) The powers of a special administrator cease on issuance of letters to a general personal representative or as otherwise directed by the court. (b) The special administrator shall promptly deliver to the general personal representative: (1) All property of the estate in the possession of the special administrator. The court may authorize the special administrator to complete a sale or other transaction affecting property in the possession of the special administrator. (2) A list of all creditor claims of which the special administrator has knowledge. The list shall show the name and address of each creditor, the amount of the claim, and what action has been taken with respect to the claim. A copy of the list shall be filed in the court. (c) The special administrator shall account in the same manner as a general personal representative is required to account. If the same person acts as both special administrator and general personal representative, the account of the special administrator may be combined with the first account of the general personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8546 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8546 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8546.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes all three subsections of a single statutory section (§ 8546(a)-(c)) as one citation; they are not independent of one another. § 8546(a) allows termination 'as otherwise directed by the court' in addition to termination on issuance of general letters; this clause does not attempt to catalog every circumstance in which a court might end a special administrator's authority early, since the statute itself leaves that to the court's order in each case. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself terminate any special administrator's authority or determine what any particular special administrator must deliver or account for — only a court order, and the special administrator's actual compliance with it, does that.
